note.text: Drama can communicate through dialogue, action, pauses and instructions for performance. Stage directions specify features such as movement or delivery; they are not necessarily spoken by a character. An aside is conventionally not heard by specified other characters. A soliloquy gives access to private thought, often when a character speaks as if alone; actual staging can vary. Dramatic irony arises when the audience knows a relevant fact that a character does not, making words or actions carry an additional meaning. Identify what each participant can know before explaining an effect.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to interpret a short script by separating spoken words, performance instructions and audience knowledge. Builds on: story features, point of view and evidence in the earlier foundation lesson. Leads to: reading the prescribed play with the teacher-confirmed edition and scene divisions.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original invented script: [Bih puts an unsigned notice in a folder. Ayuk enters.] AYUK: “The notice has already been approved.” BIH [aside; Ayuk does not hear]: “The signature is still missing.” The audience has seen and heard a gap in Ayuk’s knowledge. This can create concern about his confidence. The script does not prove why the signature is absent or what the group will decide. This is written preparation; the screen does not assess acting or listening.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Separate dialogue from directions. Map what the audience knows, what a character knows and which instruction establishes that difference. Explain the possible effect with a detail. Do not treat every long speech as a soliloquy or assume that a character’s belief is the play’s confirmed truth.

key_words.meaning: words spoken by characters in the dramatic exchange
a written instruction guiding performance or stage action
a speech conventionally unheard by specified other characters
a speech presenting private thought, often as if a character were alone
an important difference between audience and character knowledge

mistake.wrong: Every spoken belief must be a confirmed fact of the play.
mistake.right: dialogue: words spoken by characters in the dramatic exchange.
mistake.why: A character can be mistaken; compare the line with other evidence.

worked_example.problem: In the original Learn script, explain why Ayuk’s confidence can create dramatic irony.
steps: The audience receives the information that the signature is missing.
The instruction says Ayuk does not hear the aside.
His confident approval claim therefore has an additional meaning for the audience.
worked_example.answer: The gap between audience knowledge and Ayuk’s belief can create concern; the missing signature’s cause remains unknown.

cards.idea: Distinguish the ideas used in this lesson.
example: dialogue: words spoken by characters in the dramatic exchange.
stage direction: a written instruction guiding performance or stage action.
aside: a speech conventionally unheard by specified other characters.
soliloquy: a speech presenting private thought, often as if a character were alone.
dramatic irony: an important difference between audience and character knowledge.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: AYUK: The notice has already been approved is a spoken line in the invented script.
Ayuk enters tells a performer about movement.
The instruction explicitly says Ayuk does not hear Bih’s short comment.
An invented character speaks their private uncertainty as if alone.
The audience knows about the missing signature while Ayuk confidently assumes approval.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: Every spoken belief must be a confirmed fact of the play. Correction: A character can be mistaken; compare the line with other evidence.
Every stage direction must be recited as the character’s dialogue. Correction: The instruction guides action and need not be spoken.
An aside automatically makes every character know the secret. Correction: The stated convention keeps the information from Ayuk in this model.
Every speech to a group is automatically a soliloquy because it is long. Correction: Private thought and dramatic convention matter; length alone does not decide.
Dramatic irony requires the audience and character to know exactly the same facts. Correction: The significant gap in knowledge creates the additional meaning.

pick.q: Original invented script: [Amina slips the only key into her bag and exits. Bih enters.] BIH: “The key is safely on the hook.” What creates dramatic irony?
pick.r: The audience saw the key moved, while Bih speaks from incomplete knowledge.
w: Bih knows everything the audience has seen.
The stage direction is an instruction for the audience to take a real key.
The script proves Amina’s whole motive and future.
e: Bih’s claim conflicts with what the audience saw.
The direction describes fictional stage action.
The action alone does not establish all motives or outcomes.
pick.y: Explain the relevant difference in knowledge.

pick.q: Original invented script: BIH [aside; Ayuk cannot hear]: “I have not checked the date.” AYUK: “Then we agree it is accurate.” Which interpretation respects the convention?
pick.r: The audience receives Bih’s uncertainty without Ayuk receiving that aside.
w: Ayuk must have heard the aside because the audience did.
The aside guarantees the date is wrong.
The instruction erases every possible performance choice in every play.
e: Audience access and character access differ here by explicit instruction.
Unverified does not mean proven false.
This model specifies a local convention, not every staging of every play.
pick.y: Separate access to information from proof of its truth.

pick.q: Original invented script: [Alone, Amina speaks her private doubt.] AMINA: “Should I admit the unfinished work?” Which feature best fits this written model?
w: An ordinary conversation addressed to a group of classmates.
A stage direction spoken instead of every word in the speech.
Proof that all real performances must place no other actor anywhere on stage.
e: The model says alone and gives private deliberation.
The bracketed instruction and spoken words have separate roles.
Production choices vary; this is the convention specified for this example.
pick.y: The instruction and reflective question support the classification.

pick.q: Original invented script: [Pause. Bih looks at the unsigned page.] AYUK: “Why have you stopped?” Which claim is best supported?
pick.r: The pause and gaze can draw attention to the page before the question.
w: Bih’s exact thoughts and a later confession are already given.
Pause is necessarily a word Bih must pronounce.
The audience has been told the signature was deliberately forged.
e: The direction does not state those thoughts or future action.
The direction controls performance rather than requiring that spoken word.
No forgery or intention is stated.
pick.y: A performance instruction supports a possible effect without revealing every motive.
